summary:
Togo criminalises consensual same-sex sexual activity between men and between women. Human Dignity Trust's country profile records a maximum penalty of three years' imprisonment plus a fine. The 2015 Penal Code defines the offence in Article 393 as an indecent or unnatural act committed with a person of the same sex, punishable by one to three years' imprisonment and a fine of one to three million CFA francs. The Penal Code of 13 August 1980 imposed the same custodial range with a lower fine of 100,000 to 500,000 CFA francs, and the prohibition dates to 1884, when it was introduced under the German Togoland protectorate.

Advocacy is separately criminalised. Article 392 of the 2015 Penal Code punishes LGBTQ advocacy expressed through spoken words, writing or images deemed to violate public decency. The United States Department of State's 2023 human rights report reads the statutory ban on "promotion of same-sex conduct" as reaching advocacy and gender identity expression, and records that the law was enforced. Violence and threats targeting LGBTTQI persons are listed among significant human-rights issues in that department's 2022 and 2023 reports on Togo.

There is no legal route to change the gender marker on government documents in Togo. No statute prohibits discrimination on the basis of gender identity, and none prohibits it on the basis of sexual orientation.

No law explicitly bans cross-dressing, yet presentation-based arrests of transgender people are documented. A transgender person was arrested in March 2018 for supposed cross-dressing. In 2023 Bobo Períta, a TikTok influencer known for cross-dressing, was arrested for violating public decency, convicted on 1 June 2023 and sentenced to civil prison in Lomé.

In November 2019 police followed a transgender person to her home and refused to let her leave until she had sex with them. The sexual assault was prevented only by the presence of the victim's mother. That 2019 case is the most recent instance of trans-specific police violence documented in this record; no later instance is documented.

Enforcement also runs through neutral offences. Arbitrary arrests and a disproportionate use of loitering and immorality provisions against LGBTQ people are recorded, including the January 2021 arrest and imprisonment of a gay man and his partner until Afrique Arc-En-Ciel paid for their release. A Washington Blade feature published on 31 August 2015, based on interviews conducted in March 2015 and a return visit to Lomé, describes the capital's police as "particularly merciless when dealing with LGBT locals and tourists" and records a 2008 attack on the author at a site he revisited. It is the only on-the-ground account of tourist exposure to Lomé policing in this record, and it is a decade old.

Custody and care carry documented risks. Prison chaplains have refused communion to LGBTQ prisoners who have not repented for homosexuality, and LGBTQ prisoners are denied HIV/AIDS treatment and condoms. Providers at HIV and STD treatment centres discriminate against LGBTQ patients, and the resulting avoidance of care is documented. The 2022 US State Department report separately lists cruel treatment, harsh prison conditions, arbitrary detention and criminal libel enforcement among significant human-rights issues.

Protection machinery is limited. Article 5 of the Press and Communications Code Law 2020-001 prohibits dissemination of defamatory comments, including homophobic defamation. Decree No. 2023-116/PR, at Articles 17, 27 and 39, requires passenger screening by the Passenger Information Unit to be non-discriminatory and not based on sexual life or sexual orientation, and protects sexual orientation in data processing. Neither provision is stated to extend to gender identity.

Impunity is documented. The US State Department's 2011 human rights report for Togo records security-force torture and impunity alongside official and societal discrimination against members of the LGBT community. Mistreatment by civilians or state authorities tends to go unpunished, and stigma together with the risk of legal consequences from the criminalisation of same-sex conduct and LGBTQ advocacy deters victims from reporting.
tangentialFactors:
Religion is a documented driver of stigmatisation in Togo. Catholic bishops have blamed misfortunes and disasters on homosexuality, and religious programmes are used to perform conversion therapy.

A figure of 33 reported instances of human-rights violations against LGBTQ people in 2020 appears in the record. The source itself describes that number as most likely a small fraction of overall cases, and it is a raw count with no denominator, so it supports no comparison of Togo against other jurisdictions or against the general level of violence.

The adjacent turbulence recorded for Togo is not specific to LGBTQ people: harsh prison conditions, arbitrary detention, cruel treatment, criminal libel enforcement and security-force torture appear in the same reporting that documents LGBT mistreatment. A visitor detained on any charge enters that environment.

The criminal penalty structure has been stable in its custodial range across the 1980 and 2015 codes, with the fine raised in 2015 from 100,000-500,000 to one to three million CFA francs. The 2015 redefinition of the offence in Article 393 and the addition of the advocacy offence in Article 392 are the operative text a visitor faces today.
localsOnly:
An active documentation and assistance channel exists for residents. The Togolese association AAEC, with Synergia, submitted an alternative report to the UN Human Rights Committee in June 2021 stating that it works on HIV within MSM-TG populations under the National Strategic Plan 2016-2020, documents LGBT rights violations across Togo and francophone West Africa, and provides legal and judicial support to victims.

LGBTQ organisations may register as health organisations but not as LGBTQ advocacy organisations, which constrains how resident advocacy can be constituted.

Discrimination against LGBTQ residents in employment, housing, education and healthcare is documented, including refusal of housing, family rejection and denial of healthcare. People with HIV face additional discrimination, such as expulsion by family and the viewing of illness as moral punishment.

Advocacy offences bear directly on residents: Article 392 exposes spoken words, writing or images to prosecution, and enforcement includes arbitrary arrests under neutral loitering and immorality provisions. The January 2021 imprisonment of a gay man and his partner, released only after Afrique Arc-En-Ciel paid, illustrates the cost carried by residents and the organisations that fund their release.
outOfScopeNotes:
The record contains no documented statement about societal tolerance of transgender people specifically. Statements on societal attitudes in this dossier are framed around LGBTQ people generally, and the trans-specific material consists of the March 2018 arrest, the June 2023 cross-dressing conviction and the November 2019 police coercion described above.

Whether any administrative or judicial route exists to alter a gender marker, beyond the record's statement that no legal way exists, is not sourced here. The same applies to whether a change of marker would be refused in practice by a named authority.

The non-discrimination language of Decree No. 2023-116/PR is framed on sexual life and sexual orientation. Whether that decree's screening and data-protection guarantees reach gender identity is unresolved in this record, as is whether any complaint has been brought under it.

Whether Article 392's advocacy offence has been charged against a transgender person, as distinct from gay or lesbian advocacy, is not sourced. The documented trans-specific prosecutions rest on public decency and cross-dressing presentation instead.

The Washington Blade account of Lomé policing rests on one journalist's 2015 reporting, including a 2008 attack on the author. No later on-the-ground description of how Lomé police treat foreign visitors is sourced, and the account should be read as dated rather than as a current measurement.
